subject: maths
title: Very small and very large units

scenes.heading: Very small and very large units
scenes.say: A virus is tiny and a hard drive holds huge amounts of data. Scientists use special prefixes so they don’t have to write long strings of zeros. Let’s learn them.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.science: 3 mm = 3000 µm: same length, different-sized unit
scenes.breaks: Money units jump by different amounts; metric prefixes always jump by 1000.
scenes.say: A thousand dollars can be a thousand one-dollar coins or ten hundred-dollar notes. Same money, different-sized units. Prefixes work the same way: three millimetres is the same as three thousand micrometres. Bigger unit, smaller number.

scenes.heading: The prefix staircase
scenes.say: Here are the prefixes as a staircase. Tera, giga, mega and kilo at the top, then the base unit, then milli, micro and nano at the bottom. Going down one stair to a smaller unit, multiply by a thousand. Going up, divide by a thousand.

scenes.heading: Two steps down
scenes.question: Convert 0.000 045 m to micrometres.
scenes.say: Convert zero point zero zero zero zero four five metres to micrometres. That is two steps down. Times a thousand gives zero point zero four five millimetres. Times a thousand again gives forty-five micrometres.
scenes.caption: 0.000 045 m to µm is two steps down. × 1000 gives 0.045 mm; × 1000 again gives 45 µm.

scenes.heading: Download time
scenes.question: A 1.8 GB file downloads at 12 MB per second. How long does it take?
scenes.say: A one point eight gigabyte file downloads at twelve megabytes per second. First match the units: one thousand eight hundred megabytes. Then divide by the speed: one hundred and fifty seconds, or two and a half minutes.
scenes.caption: Match units: 1.8 GB = 1800 MB. 1800 ÷ 12 = 150 s, or 2.5 minutes.

scenes.heading: Reading a scale bar
scenes.say: Here is a cell under a microscope. On the screen the cell is six centimetres long, and the scale bar is two point four centimetres and stands for ten micrometres. Two and a half scale bars fit across the cell, so it is twenty-five micrometres long.
scenes.caption: The cell is 6 cm on screen; the scale bar is 2.4 cm and stands for 10 µm. 2.5 bars fit, so the cell is 25 µm long.

scenes.heading: Small m or capital M?
scenes.say: Watch the capital letters. Small m means milli, a thousandth. Capital M means mega, a million. They are a billion times apart!

points: T, G, M, k, base, m, µ, n
scenes.say: Quick recap. The prefixes go tera, giga, mega, kilo, then milli, micro, nano, and each step is a thousand. To a smaller unit, multiply. To a bigger unit, divide. And match units before dividing. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Tera, giga, mega, kilo, base, milli, micro, nano: each step is × 1000. Smaller unit: multiply. Bigger unit: divide. Match units first. Now try the practice questions!
